topic.name: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Polar Curves

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} (x+y) \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = \sin{\theta}\:$ for $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac\pi 2?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin{\theta} \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin{\theta} \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin{\theta} \cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= \sin^2{\theta}. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sin{\theta} \cos\theta$ and $y=\sin^2{\theta}$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = x+y$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \sin{\theta} \cos\theta + \sin^2{\theta} \\[5pt] &= \sin{\theta}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta). \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( \sin{\theta} \right) = \cos{\theta}, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{\left( \sin{\theta} \right)^2 + \left( \cos{\theta} \right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{ 1} \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}(x+y)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin{\theta}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta) \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin{\theta}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta) \,\textrm{d}\theta . \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} (x^2-y^2) \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = \sqrt3\:$ for $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{4}?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta = \sqrt3 \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta = \sqrt3 \sin {\theta}. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt3 \cos\theta$ and $y=\sqrt3 \sin{\theta}$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = x^2-y^2$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \left( \sqrt3 \cos\theta \right)^2 - \left( \sqrt3 \sin\theta\right)^2 \\[3pt] &= 3\cos^2\theta - 3\sin^2{\theta} \\[3pt] &= 3\left(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2{\theta}\right) \\[3pt] &= 3 \cos 2{\theta}. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( \sqrt3 \right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{\left( \sqrt3 \right)^2 + 0^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt3. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}(x^2-y^2)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/4} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}3\cos2{\theta} \cdot \sqrt3 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3\sqrt3\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos2{\theta} \,\textrm{d}\theta . \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} xy\, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = {2}\cos\theta \: $ for $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= {2} \cos\theta \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 2\cos^2\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= {2} \cos\theta\cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 2\sin\theta\cos\theta. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x= 2\cos^2\theta $ and $y=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = x y$, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= 2\cos^2\theta \cdot 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 4 \cos^3\theta\sin\theta. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left( 2\cos\theta\right) = -2\sin\theta, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{ (2\cos\theta)^2 + (-2\sin\theta)^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{4(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)}\\[5pt] &= \sqrt{4}\\[5pt] &=2. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C} xy\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 4 \cos^3\theta\sin\theta \cdot 2 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= 8 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos^3\theta\sin\theta \,\textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} x(1-y^2) \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = 1\:$ for $0 \le \theta \le\dfrac{ \pi}8?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] & = \sin \theta. \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos{\theta}$ and $y=\sin{\theta}$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}8.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = x(1-y^2) $, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \cos\theta \left( 1-\sin^2\theta\right) \\[5pt] &= \cos\theta\cdot\cos^2\theta \\[5pt] &=\cos^3{\theta}. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left(1\right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{1^2 +0^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{ 1+0} \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}x(1-y^2)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{0}^{\pi/8} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/8} \cos^3{\theta} \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/8} \cos^3{\theta} \,\textrm{d}\theta . \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} xy(1-x^2) \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = 1\:$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}8 \le \theta \le\dfrac{ \pi}4?$
question.explanation:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

\[ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. \]

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

\begin{align*} x &= r \cos\theta \\[5pt] &=1 \cdot \cos\theta \\[5pt] &= \cos\theta, \\[10pt] y &= r \sin\theta \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot \sin\theta \\[5pt] & = \sin \theta . \end{align*}

So, along our curve, we have $x= \cos{\theta}$ and $y= \sin{\theta}$, where $-\dfrac{\pi}{8} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}4.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = xy(1-x^2) $, we obtain

\begin{align*} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) &= \cos\theta\cdot \sin\theta \cdot \left( 1-\cos^2\theta\right) \\[5pt] &= \cos\theta\cdot\sin\theta\cdot \sin^2\theta \\[5pt] &=\sin^3{\theta}\cos\theta. \end{align*}

Next, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta} \left(1\right) = 0, \end{align*}

and therefore

\begin{align*} \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta &= \sqrt{(1)^2 +0^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{ 1+0} \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \displaystyle\int_\limits{C}xy(1-x^2)\,\textrm{d}s &= \int_{-\pi/8}^{\pi/4} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\\[5pt] & = \int_{-\pi/8}^{\pi/4}\sin^3{\theta}\cos\theta \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{-\pi/8}^{\pi/4} \sin^3{\theta}\cos\theta \,\textrm{d}\theta . \end{align*}
